blogs.title: Intrinsic vs. Propensity: The Eighth Circuit's Broad Definition of 'Continuous Possession' in Firearm Cases
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Eighth Circuit's rigorous application of Federal Rule of Evidence 404(b) in *United States v. Cutbank*. The court held that witness testimony regarding a defendant possessing a specific sawed-off rifle weeks or months prior to the charged incident constituted 'intrinsic evidence' rather than impermissible character evidence. By relying heavily on *United States v. Battle*, the opinion reinforces a circuit-specific trend where proof of prior possession is deemed essential to establishing the element of 'knowing possession' itself, effectively narrowing the scope of 404(b) defenses in firearm prosecutions. The post explores the tension between preventing unfair prejudice and ensuring juries have full context on the continuity of criminal conduct.

blogs.title: When Hearsay Meets Cross-Examination: Reconciling Officer Testimony with the Confrontation Clause
blogs.description: Focusing on procedural due process, this entry dissects Cutbank's challenge regarding officer testimony about statements made by victims before trial. The Eighth Circuit affirmed that admitting such hearsay for the limited purpose of explaining police conduct does not violate the Confrontation Clause so long as the declarant testifies at trial and is subject to cross-examination. This analysis highlights the practical reality of federal trials where officers often recount initial victim accounts to contextualize their investigation, provided limiting instructions are available or given at closing. The post examines why the court found no abuse of discretion in denying a pre-testimony limiting instruction and discusses the strategic implications for defense counsel managing hearsay objections in domestic violence contexts.

blogs.title: The Overlap Problem: Applying USSG § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) Enhancements Amidst Armed Career Criminal Act Convictions
blogs.description: This blog post tackles a nuanced sentencing doctrine: whether a four-level enhancement for possessing a firearm 'in connection with another felony' is permissible when that underlying felony conduct already serves as an aggravating factor for an Armed Career Criminal Act (ACCA) mandatory minimum. While ACCA mandates a statutory floor, this analysis focuses on how *Cutbank* clarifies that guideline calculations can still layer enhancements based on the same factual predicate if they address distinct aspects of culpability (e.g., risk creation vs. predicate status). The post evaluates the court's rejection of Cutbank's argument that such stacking violates 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a)'s requirement for proportionality, emphasizing the appellate deference afforded to district courts weighing § 3553(a) factors within an advisory range.
